China’s funding of global development institutions rises tenfold since 2010 to $3 billion

This makes China the fifth-largest donor to the International Development Association, which is the World Bank’s fund for the poorest countries.

Aakriti Handa

14 October, 2026 07:07 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: China’s funding to development-focussed multilateral institutions increased to more than $3 billion in 2024, registering a ten-fold increase from $260 million in 2010, according to a study conducted by the Center for Global Development.

This makes China the fifth-largest donor to the International Development Association (IDA), which is the World Bank’s fund for the poorest countries, up from the 28th position it held in 2010.

China rose the ranks thanks to its latest pledge of a whopping $1.5 million to the latest replenishment. China’s funding to multilateral development banks or MDBs — that provide grants and loans on favourable terms to poorer countries — has increased by 92% over the past five years. MDBs are funded by multiple countries to finance large development projects that emerging economies may struggle to fund alone.

Show Full Article

The study, authored by Beata Cichocka and Ian Mitchell, also found a sharp increase in China’s multilateral climate-finance footprint, from $600 million in 2017 to $5.25 billion in 2025.

Although China’s contributions to the development-oriented multilaterals have grown more than tenfold since 2010, they remain highly selective. In other words, China is not uniformly amping up funding across various multilateral banks.

China’s contributions to development-oriented multilaterals, 2011–2024 | Screenshot: Center for Global Development study titled ‘China in the Multilateral Development System’ It ranks only 19th for voluntary contributions to the United Nations and contributes to just seven of the 26 vertical funds (like Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance; the Global Fund; or the Green Climate Fund). Its funding is concentrated in MDB concessional windows that provide loans on more generous terms, especially the International Development Association, and in climate finance. Hence, China remains a modest vertical fund donor and a limited voluntary UN funder.

Its overall contributions to vertical funds have fallen by 32 per cent.

More funding; less borrowing At the same time, China is borrowing less from development banks—its borrowing from MDBs has fallen nearly by half, from over $8 billion in 2021 to $4.7 billion in 2024. At the World Bank too, China has plummeted from being the largest borrower in 2017 to only the 18th largest borrower in 2025. In fact, the World Bank estimates that China will stop borrowing altogether after 2031.

China’s borrowing from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), a multilateral development bank it helped establish and is its largest shareholder, has also declined markedly since 2017.

However, China’s growing financial contribution has not led to it becoming more influential at these development banks. China’s voting power has largely remained unchanged since 2021.

Despite holding 6 per cent of the shares in the World Bank, it holds lesser voting power than the around 12 per cent implied by the Bank’s own shareholding formula.

In addition, Chinese nationals now hold fewer top UN jobs than they did five years ago, having lost leadership positions at WHO, ITU, UNIDO and WMO. Chinese nationals lead just two of the 56 development-relevant UN bodies examined and make up only 1.3 percent of the wider UN staff, despite China accounting for around 17 percent of the world’s population.

China is indeed neither withdrawing from the existing multilateral system nor simply replacing traditional Western donors within it. It is becoming more deeply embedded across a range of institutions—notably, the World Bank’s IDA and WHO—while engaging on terms that preserve its flexibility.

AI models could soon replicate themselves across smart TVs, fridges, Anthropic warns

Researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman found that AI models can run on unfamiliar hardware and that one tested model achieved end-to-end replication in a simplified environment.

Himanshi Aggarwal

14 October, 2026 06:41 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

OpenAI and Anthropic logos in illustration | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Anthropic researchers have warned that AI models could soon be able to replicate themselves autonomously, even without access to external data centres.

New research from Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team has found that small artificial intelligence models could independently copy themselves across commercial Internet of Things (IoT) devices, such as smart TVs, fridges, vacuum cleaners and ovens.

The findings, published on 12 October and authored by researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, report that models with around 9 billion parameters already show a strong ability to set up and run inference (the process of generating outputs) on a wide range of unfamiliar hardware. By the end of this year, smaller models, too, could achieve full end-to-end self-replication.

Show Full Article

“Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes,” the research paper states.

The research also highlights the risks posed by such replication.

“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days),” the researchers explain. “Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”

Traditional computer worms copy code from one machine to another. An “AI worm” could carry its own model weights (or re-download them) and then run inference on newly infected hardware. This could result in autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA)—an AI system that deploys and spreads itself without human control.

The research focused on low-powered, poorly secured consumer devices.

In the experiments, smaller models succeeded in setting themselves up and running on a range of different devices. More capable models completed the full cycle more effectively, scanning a network, transferring themselves and launching new copies. Only the most advanced model among those tested achieved consistent end-to-end replication in a simplified environment.

“Only GLM-5.2 out of our set of tested open-weight models is capable of full end-to-end replication,” the paper states.

The researchers estimate that smaller models could reach a similar level of competence by the end of the year. By then, models small enough to run on ordinary IoT hardware could become capable of spreading on their own.

However, the spread is likely to be slow.

“As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days,” the paper states.

While a single replication cycle might take a day or two, a large number of infected devices could support many simultaneous copies of the AI. The resulting network could be comparable in scale to past IoT botnets that compromised millions of devices.

Unlike conventional malware, self-replicating AI malware might be able to figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. Traditional botnets usually target specific types of devices using fixed instructions. In the experiments, success rates improved when later versions of a model inherited notes from earlier attempts.

Anthropic also outlines several possible defences.

Unusual network traffic caused by model transfers and device-to-device communication could be detected by internet service providers. Quarantining infected networks, as was done to contain earlier botnets, has proved effective in the past. Stronger security defaults from device manufacturers, already required in some countries, could also reduce the pool of vulnerable targets.

“The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication,” the researchers conclude. “Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain.”

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

IMF calls for US to cut deficits amid bond woes, urges China to shift away from exports

Reuters

14 October, 2026 05:01 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By David Lawder and Andrea Shalal BANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) – The United States cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt without tax or spending adjustments, while China must pivot from export-led growth towards more domestic consumption, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.

Georgieva admonished the world’s two largest economies to make painful policy changes to reduce growing fiscal and trade imbalances, as her fiscal affairs chief said inflation, high debt levels and rising yields had heightened the urgency for budget consolidation around the globe.

Speaking at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva singled out advanced economies, namely the US and European countries, as the “worst offenders” on excessive debts, with higher benchmark yields spilling over to low-income countries that have already been forced by financial markets to rein in borrowing.

Show Full Article

Asked at a press conference whether the US needs tighter fiscal policy, Georgieva said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recognizes that US deficit and debt levels are too high and need to be made more sustainable.

“The authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States” to help reduce debt, Georgieva said.

“At the Fund, we believe that growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments. So, some (fiscal) measures would be necessary.”

The call for more action to reduce debt was echoed in the IMF’s Fiscal Monitor report on Wednesday, which warned that delays in an era of higher borrowing costs would only make the job harder in coming years.

While that message is a perennial one from the IMF, Rodrigo Valdes, the head of the IMF’s Fiscal Affairs department, said the surge in bond yields had left governments with little fiscal room to manoeuvre.

“We dialled up the urgency of our message,” he added.

BESSENT NO-SHOW

Bessent is not attending the annual meetings in Bangkok, despite this year’s US presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, instead favouring domestic engagements as the US midterm election campaign heats up.

He has acted as a chief spokesman for President Donald Trump’s economic policies, particularly touting the deep tax cuts passed last year by Republicans now trying to maintain control of the US Congress.

G20 finance ministers are due to meet on the sidelines of the Bangkok meetings on Thursday. The US has used its G20 presidency to try to rally allies to take stronger action to counter China’s “non-market” economic policies that have led to excess industrial capacity and a flood of global exports.

Asked about imbalances emanating from China, on a day when data showed it was on track to post a record trade surplus, Georgieva repeated longstanding advice to Beijing: “For surplus countries, what they need to do is increase domestic consumption. That clearly applies to China’s growth model. Shift from exports more toward domestic consumption.”

Deficit countries need to save more and spend less, while Europe needs to invest more in competitiveness, she said.

“To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more, and Europe has to invest more,” Georgieva added.

FRENCH FISCAL WORRIES

This week’s meetings have been dominated by worries about growing debt and rising bond yields and risks from the artificial intelligence boom.

France, one of the advanced economies worst hit by a global bond sell-off, needs to solve its own debt woes through fiscal consolidation, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said, effectively playing down speculation about an ECB intervention in the bond market.

Asked at a CNN event in Bangkok whether the ECB was about to help France, Lagarde said it was up to Paris to soothe investors’ nerves. “And for that one, the primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies,” she said.

The IMF has lauded Britain for taking steps toward consolidation, but made clear on Wednesday that it does not want London to accelerate the pace of fiscal consolidation. “Our recommendation is ‘stay the course’,” Valdes said.

Still, OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann called for “strong fiscal discipline” in a statement to the IMF’s steering committee, saying this was needed to ensure stability.

“In every G20 country except Germany and Türkiye, public debt as a share of GDP was higher in the first quarter of 2026 than at the end of 2007,” he wrote to the International Monetary and Financial Committee.

“Countries need to contain and reallocate spending, improve public-sector efficiency and make tax systems more effective. They should also protect investment that drives future growth, especially in education, skills and digital infrastructure.”

CALLS TO AID POOR COUNTRIES

Regarding the growing divergence between advanced countries benefiting from AI investment and those bypassed by it, highlighted in Tuesday’s IMF economic forecasts, Georgieva also urged IMF member countries to fully fund IMF facilities for low-income and vulnerable countries.

These include the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which provides low- and zero-interest loans to low-income countries, and the Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust, a fund that provides grants for debt-service relief and cancellation to the poorest and most vulnerable member countries, she said.

These countries, too, were being squeezed by higher bond yields, with average debt service costs that have increased to 14% of revenue from 6% a decade ago, even as overall debt burdens have eased, she said.

“The risk of divergence is most dangerous for those that are already further behind,” Georgieva added.

(Reporting by David Lawder and Andrea Shalal; Editing by John Mair, Shri Navaratnam, Toby Chopra)

As Ebola spreads in eastern Congo, mothers and children shun vital care

Reuters

14 October, 2026 03:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Gradel Muyisa Mumbere and Clement Bonnerot BUTEMBO, Democratic Republic of Congo, Oct 14 (Reuters) – The fear of Ebola is keeping women and children from seeking healthcare in eastern Congo, health workers and aid agencies say, contributing to soaring maternal deaths and falling childhood immunization rates that could strain the healthcare system for years to come.

Health workers say that misplaced anxiety about contact with Ebola is the primary reason women are forgoing crucial prenatal care and opting to give birth at home, and dying more often in the event of complications.

There is still limited data available but figures for Ituri province are raising alarm. UN figures show that maternal deaths in Ituri province soared nearly 70% between May and July compared with a year earlier, a troubling indicator of the impact of the Ebola outbreak — currently Congo’s worst on record — on the primary healthcare system.

Show Full Article

Steep international aid cuts have also led to shortages of some life-saving medications.

In eastern Butembo city, nurses at the Masiki healthcare center told Reuters that births have fallen sharply at their maternity ward since the Ebola outbreak was declared in May. Just one mother was resting with her newborn during a recent visit, among rows of empty beds.

“They think the medicines we give them contain the Ebola virus,” head nurse Liliane Adronga told Reuters — highlighting just one of many unfounded suspicions circulating about the virus and healthcare.

Adronga described how women often avoided seeking care until it was too late, recalling a recent case where a woman was believed to have lost her baby while suffering from untreated malaria.

The UNFPA has reported a more than 30% drop in hospital deliveries and 50% drop in treatment for obstetric complications for the May to July period since the outbreak began.

CHILDREN MISSING ROUTINE VACCINES

The Ebola outbreak has spread across seven provinces, infecting more than 8,000 people and killing over 4,000. Officials say it is far from being contained, although infections have slowed in parts of the country.

Routine data collection is a growing challenge but aid agencies say data for the first three months of the outbreak shows a sharp fall in routine childhood vaccinations and paediatric visits.

UNICEF warned in August that routine vaccinations fell by more than half across Ebola hot spots in Ituri between April and June. In Mongbwalu, first-dose measles vaccinations declined by 69%.

“We should be concerned not only about the direct impact of Ebola, but also its indirect effects on health, nutrition, child protection and insecurity,” said Raoul Kamadjeu, a public health emergencies expert at UNICEF. “The longer an epidemic persists, the greater the risks.”

Congo has long struggled with recurring measles outbreaks for example, with tens of thousands of cases recorded every year, and 126,000 cases so far in 2026, according to data by Congo’s health ministry.

UNICEF says that across the province, health facilities administered 23,000 fewer routine vaccine doses in May and June than in April.

MISINFORMATION, SUPERSTITION ADDING TO CONCERNS

For some parents, concerns about Ebola overshadowed the benefits of vaccination.

“We didn’t want to bring our children to health facilities for fear of being referred to an Ebola treatment center. Because once you end up there, you can die,” said Masika Furaha, a mother of three in Butembo. She did in the end have her youngest child vaccinated after seeing that children who received the shots remained healthy.

Dr. Mupenzi Mumbere, a paediatrician in Butembo, said misinformation is contributing to the fears among parents with sometimes tragic consequences. He described an episode in which a mother burst into tears when he referred her son to the main hospital for an X-ray because she believed staff would take him and kill him with Ebola.

Many parents first try self-medication or seek help from traditional healers before eventually turning to hospitals, he said, often with devastating consequences.

“That’s when I realised how great the misunderstanding was,” said Mumbere. “In the worst cases, children arrive in such poor condition that there is little left to do but watch them die.”

(Reporting by Gradel Muyisa Mumbere in Butembo; Additional reporting by Jessica Donati and Clement Bonnerot; writing by Clement Bonnerot; Editing by Robbie Corey-Boulet, Jessica Donati, Alexandra Hudson)
